Inside the apps

From a reading list
to a research project.

Built for research that develops over months: reading primary and secondary sources, returning to passages, drafting chapters, and planning the next session.

  1. Organize what you need to read.

    Find books and papers by title or author, filter by tags, and distinguish collected, to-read, reading, and finished items. Open a reading record to work with its metadata, local PDF, and citation files.

  2. Return to the passage behind a note.

    Capture quotations with page references in a reading record. Keep research notes beside the PDF, and reopen the linked Archive record when you need its wider context.

  3. Develop notes into a manuscript.

    Draft chapters in the manuscript workspace with headings, footnotes, citations, and figures. For writing in Microsoft Word, the companion add-in provides library search, citations, footnotes, endnotes, and bibliographies.

  4. Give a long project a daily rhythm.

    Set the day’s Big 3 and a first action, then use the weekly planner to arrange research tasks, meetings, and reading. Daily records keep previous work available when you return to the project.

Academia Archive.Keep the source and its context.

A source library for humanities and social science research: photographs, scans, PDFs, books, and archival records, with the descriptive details that make them usable as evidence.

  • Describe the kind of source you have.Use fields suited to books, journal articles, and archival material. Keep author and contributor roles, dates, publication details, identifiers, and attachments with the record.
  • Keep passages close to their source.Record transcriptions, quotations, and research notes for a source, attached file, or image region. Search metadata, notes, and local OCR text together.
  • Work across your existing tools.Organize sources into collections and tags. Bring in Tropy exports and Zotero records, connect selected sources to Flow, and use the Word connection for citation work.

Simple PDF.Read the argument.
Keep the endnotes in view.

A focused macOS reader for the back-and-forth of scholarly reading. Keep the main text open while a separate pane shows the endnotes, and use the outline to move between chapters.

The example below shows the chapter on page 1 alongside its notes on page 10, without leaving the main text.

Small tools for
the work around research.

Alongside Flow and Archive, we develop focused local tools for notes and files. Contact us for current availability.

Simple Note
Write in a rich-text editor or Markdown, organize notes with tags and pins, and search titles and text. Open local Markdown files and export notes when you need them elsewhere.
Simple Search
A macOS menu-bar file finder with Korean initial-consonant and partial-name search, file-type filters, and Quick Look. Its index uses file names and metadata rather than reading document contents.

Optional Claude
assistance.

In-app features planned

Today: we use Claude to develop and maintain the software.

Next: optional Claude API assistance within the research workflow: ask about selected documents, compare themes across notes, and work on a draft in Korean or English.

We plan to evaluate responses against source passages and page references, while keeping the researcher in charge of what is sent and what enters their writing. Our priorities are reliable source use, privacy controls, and predictable costs. In-app API features are still planned.

Built from
graduate-student work.

HVN · Founder & Developer

Monoon Works grew out of the challenges I faced as a graduate student: keeping up with reading, organizing sources, and turning notes into an argument.

Zotero, Tropy, and EndNote each had a place in that process. Moving between them kept bringing me back to a question: how could references, source materials, notes, and writing stay connected as a research project grew?

I began developing Academia Flow in July 2025 to explore that question through software, with the needs of humanities and social science researchers at its core.

Where is my research stored?

Flow uses local storage for the research workspace. Archive keeps its source files and database locally. Optional connections, such as Zotero sync, have their own setup.

How can I try it?

The current pilot is private. Email us about your workflow and the product you are interested in, and we can discuss availability.
